turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Good heavens, what a ridiculous conversation. What's all this fuss about the address of his house in Belgrave Square? It's really most tiresome.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, her voice firm as she declared, This is an extremely serious matter, Mr. Worthing, and she would not be put off by such frivolity.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He, of course, wishes to assure Lady Bracknell that he is quite aware of the gravity of the situation and that he is endeavouring to provide the information she requires.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed slightly as she regarded Jack Worthing, her voice dripping with disdain. She had traveled a considerable distance to meet this young man, and his evasiveness was beginning to try her patience. Still, he seemed reluctant to provide any satisfactory information about his personal circumstances, and Lady Bracknell's curiosity was piqued. She leaned forward, her voice taking on a slightly sharper tone, as she pressed him for details.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen's eyes widened in exasperation as she turned to Lady Bracknell, her voice rising in incredulity. Good heavens, really, couldn't her mother see that Jack was perfectly capable of taking care of her? This was all just a silly fuss over nothing, a ridiculous overreaction to a perfectly ordinary situation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, her voice dripping with disapproval, as she declared that Mr. Worthing's behaviour was most unbecoming, and she must insist that he provide a more satisfactory explanation for his lack of candour.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He, of course, wishes to assure Lady Bracknell that he is endeavouring to provide as much information as possible, but, as a gentleman, he must also be mindful of his family's privacy and reputation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing's evasiveness is becoming increasingly tiresome, and Lady Bracknell insists that he must provide a fuller account of his personal circumstances, lest she be forced to reconsider his suitability as a suitor for her daughter's hand.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hopes, Lady Bracknell, that he may be excused further inquiry into his personal circumstances, as they are, in truth, of a somewhat delicate nature.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing's reluctance to disclose the details of his personal circumstances is a most unwelcome development, one that casts a shadow of doubt over his entire character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He dares hope, Lady Bracknell, that the burden of responsibility for his past actions may be shared with his future wife, and that Miss Gwendolen may be willing to exercise her own discretion in the matter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen was growing increasingly exasperated with this inquisition, and she wondered why her mother couldn't see that Jack was perfectly suitable as a husband, with or without a detailed account of his past.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: This intransigence, Mr. Worthing, is most unbecoming, and Lady Bracknell dares to wonder if it is an omen of a deeper moral weakness.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He humbly begs Lady Bracknell's pardon if his words have been taken amiss, and he assures her that his reluctance to disclose certain particulars is not a sign of weakness, but rather a wish to spare his betrothed unnecessary distress.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Good heavens, Lady Bracknell, can't you see that Jack is perfectly capable of taking care of himself, and of me, and that this tedious inquisition is only serving to make him uncomfortable?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed, her gaze piercing as she pondered the possibility that Mr. Worthing might be concealing some dubious information, a notion that only served to heighten her already considerable unease.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He was getting a bit flustered, and he wished he could think of a way to put Lady Bracknell's mind at ease, for he was convinced that the truth would eventually come out and prove his suitability as a husband for Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Good heavens, Lady Bracknell, Gwendolen thought, can't you see that Jack is perfectly capable of taking care of himself, and of her, and that this tedious inquisition is only serving to make him uncomfortable?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she regarded Mr. Worthing with a mixture of disdain and curiosity, her voice taking on a tone of stern disapproval: his reluctance to provide adequate information about his past was a most singular and disturbing thing, and she must insist that he be more forthcoming if he wished to prove himself a suitable husband for her daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He wished to assure Lady Bracknell that he was not hiding anything, that he would be more than happy to provide any information she deemed necessary, and that he hoped she would be able to see the sincerity in his heart.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
